content: In 2011, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended parenteral artesunate as the first-line treatment for severe malaria, replacing quinine. Before this recommendation, many countries, particularly in Africa, had already started using artemether, another artemisinin derivative. This Cochrane Review evaluates the efficacy and safety of intramuscular artemether compared to both quinine and artesunate for treating severe malaria in adults and children. The primary objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of intramuscular artemether in comparison to other parenteral treatments for severe malaria. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared intramuscular artemether with intravenous or intramuscular quinine or artesunate. The primary outcome measured was all-cause mortality. Data were collected and analyzed using risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. A total of 19 RCTs were included in the review, involving 2874 participants (adults and children) with severe malaria. These trials were conducted in Africa (12 trials) and Asia (7 trials). Artemether versus Quinine: In children, there is likely little to no difference in the risk of death between intramuscular artemether and quinine (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.21; moderate-certainty evidence). The time to coma resolution may be approximately five hours shorter with artemether compared to quinine (MD −5.45 hours, 95% CI −7.90 to −3.00; low-certainty evidence). Artemether may have little to no effect on the risk of neurological sequelae (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.07; low-certainty evidence). Parasite clearance time is likely about nine hours shorter with artemether compared to quinine (MD −9.03 hours, 95% CI −11.43 to −6.63; moderate-certainty evidence). Fever clearance time may be approximately three hours shorter with artemether compared to quinine (MD −3.73 hours, 95% CI −6.55 to −0.92; low-certainty evidence). In adults, treatment with intramuscular artemether likely results in fewer deaths compared to quinine (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.83; moderate-certainty evidence). Artemether versus Artesunate: There are no direct randomized trials comparing artemether and artesunate in children. In adults, mortality is likely higher with intramuscular artemether compared to artesunate (RR 1.80, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.97; moderate-certainty evidence). Conclusions: Artemether appears to be more effective than quinine in both children and adults for the treatment of severe malaria. However, when compared to artesunate, artemether seems to be less effective in adults, and there is insufficient evidence for children. These findings align with WHO recommendations, which prioritize artesunate as the preferred treatment for severe malaria, with artemether being an acceptable alternative when artesunate is unavailable.
